column1: What is a causal set?
column2: A set of discrete elements with a partial order that is transitive, never circular and locally finite (Dowker 2005, §2.1).

column1: In causal set theory, what gives volume?
column2: Counting elements: number gives volume, order gives causal structure (Dowker 2005, §2.3).

column1: At what scale is spacetime proposed to be discrete?
column2: Of the order of the Planck scale (Dowker 2005, §2.3).

column1: What is the Hauptvermutung?
column2: The conjecture that two continuum spacetimes approximating the same causal set are close to each other (Dowker 2005, §2.3).

column1: What does Dowker identify with the passage of time?
column2: The birth of spacetime atoms: the present is the process of birth (Dowker 2014).

column1: What is "asynchronous becoming"?
column2: Growth by births that are only partly ordered; Dowker credits the term to Sorkin (Dowker 2014).

column1: Is the birth order of spacetime atoms physical?
column2: Only where it shows in the causal order; labels are pure gauge, the discrete analogue of general covariance (Dowker 2014; Rideout & Sorkin 1999, §3).

column1: Who are the "Blockheads", and Dowker's reply?
column2: Those who run growth to infinity and call the result a static block. Reply: that is a different theory, fitting experience less well (Dowker 2014).

column1: In sequential growth, does growth happen in time?
column2: No: it is taken to constitute time, not happen in it (Rideout & Sorkin 1999, §1.1).

column1: Does sequential growth ever stop?
column2: No: every element has a descendant, a result of Henson's (Dowker 2005, §3.4).

column1: Crystallizing block: what is fixed and what is open?
column2: The past is fixed; the future does not yet exist physically; the present is where quantum outcomes become definite (Ellis & Rothman 2010).

column1: What does Rovelli put in place of time?
column2: Relations between variables; time returns statistically as "thermal time" (Rovelli 2009, §IV, §VI).

column1: Why can a universe of massless particles not keep time?
column2: Massless particles experience no passage of time, so nothing can be built into a clock (Penrose 2006, p. 2).

column1: Radiation era: how are age and temperature related?
column2: t T² = 2.4 / √N(T), with t in seconds and T in MeV (PDG, eq. 22.44).

column1: Roughly when does Α end?
column2: When the Higgs field takes its value, near 100 GeV: about 2.5 × 10⁻¹¹ s (worked from PDG eq. 22.44).

column1: When was the CMB released?
column2: At last scattering, about 370,000 years in (PDG, §22.4.1).

column1: What does Everpresent Λ predict?
column2: Λ fluctuates by about 1/√V, staying of the order of the ambient density (Ahmed et al. 2004, §II).

column1: Being versus becoming: who stands where, in Dowker's talk?
column2: Being: Parmenides, Paul Davies (flow is an illusion). Becoming: Buddhist dependent origination, John Norton (time really passes). (Talk, 19:11 to 22:24)

column1: What is Newton's spacetime made of?
column2: Stacked snapshots of three-dimensional space, with one global time and real simultaneity. (Talk, 26:07)

column1: What is Einstein's spacetime made of?
column2: Point events: no three-dimensional space, no global time, no simultaneity; time elapses only along world lines. (Talk, 35:22 to 41:53)

column1: Who is the growing block associated with?
column2: The philosopher C. D. Broad. (Talk, 49:43)

column1: About how many spacetime atoms would our observable universe need?
column2: Roughly 10^240. (Talk, 56:51)

column1: Who proposed causal sets?
column2: Independently 't Hooft, Myrheim, and Bombelli, Lee, Meyer and Sorkin; championed by Sorkin. (Talk, 56:19)

column1: Newton, Einstein, the future: what is time about in each?
column2: Space, events, process. (Talk, 59:54)
